To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the anomalous magnetic moments of the electron bound to the 12C5+, 14N6+ and 16 O7+ ions have been determined with an accuracy of 1.2 ppb, and that the electron magnetic moment has been measured in 24Mg11+, 27Al13+, 32S14+, 38Ar16+ and 40Ca18+ with an accuracy of about 100 ppm. Proc. SPI

the anomalous magnetic moments of hydrogen-like ions have been measured with a precision on the ppb-level, that the QED theory of these systems is in excellent agreement with experiment, that the results can be used for a precise determination of the electron mass me and the fine structure constant a, and that the g-factor measurements on hydrogen-like ions are a unique tool for testing the QED in the presence of strong fields and for the determination of nuclear parameters.

the anomalous magnetic moments of the electron bound to hydrogen-like ions have been measured with a precision of about 1 ppb, that the QED theory has been tested on this level, and that the results are consistent with the CODATA value of the fine structure constant.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the precise determination of the electron magnetic moment in hydrogenlike systems.
the determination of fundamental properties of matter and the development of novel experimental techniques for the investigation of highly charged ions.
the determination of atomic and nuclear parameters with unprecedented accuracy, and with the testing of fundamental theories.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the g-factor of the electron bound to a nucleus is known with a precision of better than 1 ppm in hydrogen-like ions with Z=1-92, and with a precision better than 0.1 ppm in hydrogen- and helium-like ions with Z =1-18.
the QED calculation of the electron g-factor in the hydrogen-like 12C5+, 16O7+ and 40Ca13+ ions is confirmed on a ppb level.
the present status of QED theory is very well established and that the experimental results obtained with the Penning trap technique are in agreement with QED theory on the ppmb level.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the g-factor of the electron bound to the nucleus is the most precisely known property of the hydrogen atom.
the g-factor of a single electron is now known for all elements of the periodic table.
we can now measure g-factors with a relative uncertainty of about 5 x 10-11.
The main takeaway from our work is that

a precise determination of the electron mass in the presence of strong nuclear fields can be achieved by combining g-factor measurements on different ions with different nuclear charge numbers Z and different atomic numbers A.
the precision of the measurements can be improved significantly if the systematic errors can be kept small.
the precision of the measurements can be increased by orders of magnitude, and that the precision of theoretical predictions will have to keep pace with the experimental progress.
